nature-eecon-233.title: Electronic waste: the 62 million tonne problem
nature-eecon-233.text:
In 2022 the world threw away about 62 million tonnes of electrical and electronic devices. Only 22.3% was formally collected and recycled. Electronic waste, also called WEEE or e-waste, is any such device at the end of its life, and it is a stubborn kind of {{ref:nature-eecon-231}}. The total is projected to reach 82 million tonnes by 2030.

The loss is financial as well as physical. An estimated US$62 billion of key raw materials is lost each year through inadequate recycling. Part of the problem is the shrinking lifetime of electrical goods, which repair can counter.

How the rest is handled matters. Informal recycling, much of it by hand in developing countries, exposes workers to mercury, lead and cadmium. Guiyu in China is a well-known informal processing site. Informal workshops have few automated procedures or protective equipment. Formal e-recycling facilities use automated machinery with pollution control, recovering metals and avoiding the {{ref:nature-found-079}} that hazardous disposal causes.

nature-eecon-237.title: Waste minimisation: the cheapest waste is never made
nature-eecon-237.text:
The cheapest way to manage waste is often not to create it. Waste minimisation is a set of processes and practices meant to reduce the amount of waste produced. It means redesigning products and processes, or changing consumption patterns, rather than treating waste after it arises.

The benefits are practical. Firms get more output per unit of raw material, lower purchasing costs, a better reputation and easier compliance with environmental regulation. Scrap can be fed back to the start of the line, and one process's waste can become another's raw material. Waste exchanges cut disposal volumes. Reducing waste in one stage, though, may create it in another.

Eliminating overpackaging is source reduction. The EU's packaging targets require plastic packaging cuts of 5% by 2030, 10% by 2035 and 15% by 2040. Personal waste reduction is a small part of total waste, but householders can still influence policy. One study suggests a bag tax motivates reuse more than a discount does.

nature-eecon-236.title: Biomimetics: copying nature's designs
nature-eecon-236.text: A Japanese bullet train owes its aerodynamics to a bird. The Shinkansen 500 Series was modelled on the kingfisher's beak. That is biomimetics, the replication of models, systems and elements of nature to solve complex human problems. The American biophysicist Otto Schmitt developed the concept in the 1950s. Applications range from commercial technologies to prototypes. Holistic planned grazing mimics herds moved on by predators, and its founder claims it can build soil, raise biodiversity and reverse desertification.

nature-eecon-232.title: Waste management from collection to disposal
nature-eecon-232.text: Waste management covers everything that happens to waste from its inception to its final disposal. It includes collection, transport, treatment and disposal, together with monitoring, regulation, and waste-related laws, technologies and economic mechanisms. Resource recovery uses wastes as inputs to create valuable products, reducing the need for landfill space. Energy recovery extracts heat, electricity or energy from non-recyclable waste by combustion, gasification, pyrolysis or anaerobic digestion. Together these are called waste-to-energy.

nature-eecon-234.title: The EU's WEEE and RoHS directives of 2003
nature-eecon-234.text: Europe tackled discarded electronics with two linked laws in 2003. The WEEE Directive, in force from February 2003, focused on recycling {{ref:nature-eecon-233}} and offered many collection schemes free of charge to consumers. The RoHS Directive targeted alternatives to hazardous materials such as cadmium, mercury and lead. It was revised in 2008 and 2013. One law gathers the devices back; the other cuts the poisons put into them.

nature-eecon-235.title: Ecological sanitation: toilets as nutrient loops
nature-eecon-235.text:
Human waste holds nutrients that farms need. Ecological sanitation, or ecosan, treats human excreta and wastewater as a resource, hence its other name, resource-oriented sanitation. It favors no single toilet technology. Its main objectives are to reduce health risks from sanitation, contaminated water and waste; to prevent groundwater and surface water pollution; and to reuse nutrients or energy in wastes.

The logic is partly about supply. Phosphate rock is a limited mineral resource, and one review suggested phosphate in urine could supply 22% of total demand. Urea in urine is made industrially using fossil fuels. Managing urine well can therefore cut fertilizer cost, energy use and wastewater treatment costs.

nature-gov-237.title: Marine pollution: what ends up in the ocean
nature-gov-237.text:
Early on, most scientists thought the oceans were so vast they could dilute pollution harmlessly. Significant international laws came only in the twentieth century. Marine pollution is the harmful effect in the ocean of substances humans use or spread, such as waste, particles, noise, light, excess carbon dioxide or invasive organisms.

About 80% of the waste comes from land-based activity, with marine transportation also contributing. That makes continental shelves most vulnerable. Pollution enters the sea by three main routes: direct discharge, runoff carried by rain, and release from the atmosphere.

Farm, urban and construction runoff carries nutrients that fuel algal blooms. These can use up oxygen and create hypoxic conditions. Eighty percent of marine debris is plastic, which breaks down into microplastics and nanoplastics. Persistent toxicants such as PCBs, DDT, dioxins and PFAS, and heavy metals such as mercury, lead, copper and cadmium, break down slowly or not at all. Between 1950 and 2026 the average ocean surface pH fell from about 8.15 to 8.05, with human carbon dioxide emissions the primary cause.

Pollution can reduce marine biodiversity and productivity and deplete human marine food resources. SDG Target 14.1 aims to prevent and significantly reduce marine pollution by 2025.

nature-gov-235.title: Collective action and the free-rider problem
nature-gov-235.text:
Why do rich members of a group often pay for what everyone enjoys? Mancur Olson's 1965 book The Logic of Collective Action is an early analysis of public-good costs. Collective action is action taken together by a group to improve their condition and reach a common objective. Olson argued that individuals with more resources carry a higher burden of providing a public good, while poorer ones tend to free ride, which can lead to under-provision.

Institutional designs include joint products that tie a private good to a public good, clubs that exclude non-members, and federated structures, since collaboration emerges more easily in small groups. The social identity model explains participation through perceived injustice, perceived efficacy and social identity.

nature-gov-236.title: Citizen science: research with the public
nature-gov-236.text:
Anyone with a smartphone can now add to a scientific dataset. Citizen science is research conducted with the participation of the general public or amateur and nonprofessional researchers. It is used in ecology, biology, conservation, health, astronomy and more. The term first appeared in a January 1989 MIT Technology Review issue on community labs studying environmental issues.

At the low end, contributory or crowdsourcing projects have citizens collect observations, offer computing power or install sensors. Citizen science has contributed much to biodiversity analysis, mostly species occurrence, abundance and phenology data, with birds the most observed group. Apps such as iNaturalist and Mosquito Alert vastly expanded participation.

Ethics and data governance, including data protection law and community control over reuse, are growing concerns. ECSA published Ten Principles of Citizen Science in 2015. Researchers have even estimated the monetary value of contributions, for example from seven Zooniverse projects.

nature-gov-230.title: The Half-Earth proposal
nature-gov-230.text:
E. O. Wilson wanted half the planet left to nature. His 2016 proposal was to set aside half of the Earth's surface as a human-free natural reserve to preserve biodiversity. Tony Hiss coined the name Half-Earth, and Wilson's book of that name closes a trilogy.

Reviewers split on whether the target is realistic or politically workable. A Science reviewer noted that in 2015 only 15% of land and 2.8% of marine areas were protected. Others called it more an aspirational goal than a plan, since it gives no detail on territories, funding mechanisms or agreements, or on whether people in reserves would be relocated.

nature-gov-243.title: Wildfire: destroyer and part of the cycle
nature-gov-243.text:
Over 85% of US wildfires are started by people. A wildfire is an unplanned and uncontrolled fire in an area of combustible vegetation. Ignition can also be natural: lightning, volcanic eruptions or sparks from rock-fall. Tropical farmers use slash-and-burn clearing.

Fires need ignition, fuel and oxygen. High moisture slows spread, and dense forests are less susceptible because shade lowers temperature and raises humidity. Some natural forest ecosystems depend on wildfire, and fire adaptations are traits that help plants and animals survive it or use the resources it creates. Modern forest management uses prescribed burns to cut fire risk and promote natural cycles, though they can escape containment.

Climate change promotes wildfire weather, and the carbon released adds to greenhouse gases. Climate models do not yet fully reflect this feedback. Suppression costs a large share of national output, and US agencies collectively spend tens of billions of dollars annually. Smoke carries particulate matter that harms the respiratory system, and runoff after fires can make drinking water unsafe.

nature-gov-242.title: Political economy: where politics and markets meet
nature-gov-242.text:
Adam Smith held that economic elites seek monopoly and gain political power with it. Political economy is the interdisciplinary field of political science and economics that studies how political and economic systems relate to and influence each other. Thinkers from Aristotle to Smith and Marx warned that concentrated economic power can distort politics.

The field began as state-level household management, covering wealth, production, trade and taxation. The French physiocrats were its first major exponents, followed by Smith, Malthus and Ricardo. In the late 19th century economics became a separate, mathematical discipline, and Marshall's Principles of Economics (1890) argued the field was better called economics.

Modern political economy asks how states, laws and institutions shape markets, and how markets, wealth and firms shape politics. It splits into comparative political economy, on market and state within countries, and international political economy, on global interactions. Public choice and social choice theory are closely tied to it; public choice models voters, politicians and bureaucrats as mainly self-interested. Geography studies it through human-environment interactions in which economic actions transform nature.

nature-gov-241.title: NIMBY: not in my backyard
nature-gov-241.text:
Who gets to say no to a new facility? NIMBY is opposition by residents to proposed development or infrastructure in their local area, with support for strict land use regulation. The label is used pejoratively, and those it names challenge it, saying they defend overlooked community values. It implies they object only because the project is close, so its use is inherently contentious.

A 1994 study found NIMBY movements generally oppose waste disposal, low-income housing and social services facilities. Variants include YIMBY (pro-development) and PIBBY, where privileged groups push objectionable facilities onto disadvantaged neighborhoods less able to appeal. Studies show stricter land use regulation raises housing prices; one estimate puts the cost to US workers at $1 trillion in lost wages.

nature-gov-238.title: Climate migration: people on the move
nature-gov-238.text:
UNHCR estimates an average of 20 million people a year are forcibly displaced by weather-related events. Climate migration is the movement of people driven by sudden or gradual climate-exacerbated disasters such as heavy rains, drought, desertification, environmental degradation, sea-level rise and cyclones. Most climate migrants move within their own countries, and gradual environmental shifts affect more people than sudden disasters.

The most common projection is 150-200 million people displaced by climate change by 2050, though one estimate reaches 1.2 billion. Many discussions rest on projections rather than current migration data. Migration after sudden events like hurricanes and floods is often short-distance, involuntary and temporary. Slow-onset events such as drought have more mixed effects.

Migration can be framed as a human rights issue, suggesting protection frameworks, or as a security issue, which may mean tighter border security. Few international, regional or domestic legal regimes adequately protect climate migrants. Planning means preparing for the abandonment of vulnerable areas and the arrival of vulnerable communities in cities, with locally informed, equitable approaches.

nature-gov-240.title: Environmental migrants and the numbers dispute
nature-gov-240.text:
Norman Myers projected 200 million environmental refugees by 2050, later 250 million. Critics called his work hard to check, and he admitted his figures were 'heroic extrapolation'. An environmental migrant is a person forced to leave home by sudden or long-term changes in the local or regional environment that compromise well-being or livelihood.

No uniform definition exists. Terms such as environmental refugee, climate migrant and environmentally displaced person are used interchangeably, and the distinctions between them remain contested. Lester Brown proposed 'environmental refugee' in 1976. {{ref:nature-gov-238}} describes a subset, displaced by sea-level rise, extreme weather, or drought and water scarcity. The IOM names three types: emergency migrants fleeing a disaster, forced migrants leaving deteriorating conditions, and motivated migrants who leave to avoid future problems.

Evidence is mixed. A 2014-2018 study of three deltas found most migrants cited economic reasons and only 2.8% cited the environment, though many saw rising hazard exposure. Over 65 million people live in Small Island Developing States, and an estimated 11.5 million people from them lived abroad as of 2020. Critics say these definitions overlook structural drivers such as colonial legacies and unequal resource extraction, and that marginalized communities suffer the most degradation with the least power to relocate.

nature-gov-239.title: Tribal relocation from sea-level rise
nature-gov-239.text:
Several Indigenous communities in the United States are relocating because of rising seas, erosion and flooding. They show what {{ref:nature-gov-238}} looks like for small, place-bound communities.

The Biloxi-Chitimacha-Choctaw community of Isle de Jean Charles, Louisiana, about 100 people, is being resettled with federal grant money because of saltwater intrusion and sea-level rise. The Quinault Indian Nation devised a relocation plan to move two villages, Taholah and Queets, with 660 tribal members, above tsunami and flood zones.

Relocation is costly and depends on federal funding. Moving the 471-member Shoalwater Bay Tribe is estimated to cost half a billion dollars.
